title: Storage
intro: Storage improved in two different ways, and only one of them is the number on the box. Capacity grew by roughly a million times. Response time, meaning how long you wait before the first byte arrives, improved by far less until the moving parts were removed, and that is the change you can actually feel.

blocks.title: Magnetic surfaces and a moving arm
blocks.text: A hard disk stores data as magnetised patches on spinning metal platters. To read something, an arm swings the head to the right track and then waits for the right part of the track to rotate underneath it. Both of those are physical movements measured in thousandths of a second, and no amount of clever engineering makes moving a piece of metal fast.

blocks.name: Seagate ST-506
blocks.text: The first hard disk aimed at small computers. Five megabytes for the price of a small car's deposit, and a seek time about four hundred times slower than the drive in this machine.

blocks.name: IBM PC storage as shipped
blocks.spec: Cassette tape, or one 160 KB 5.25 inch floppy
blocks.text: The base model saved to audio cassette. A hard disk was not an option on the original PC at all, and the floppy held less than a single photograph taken on a phone today.

blocks.name: IBM PC XT
blocks.spec: 10 MB hard disk, 5.25 inch full height
blocks.text: The first IBM PC with a hard disk as standard. Ten megabytes was described at the time as more than anyone would fill.

blocks.name: IDE / ATA
blocks.spec: Controller moved onto the drive, 40-pin ribbon cable
blocks.text: Before this, the drive was dumb and a separate controller card knew how to operate it. Integrating the controller onto the drive itself made drives cheaper and interchangeable, and the connector lasted until SATA replaced it eighteen years later.

blocks.name: 3.5 inch floppy, 1.44 MB
blocks.text: Smaller, tougher and roughly ten times the capacity of the original 5.25 inch disks. It stayed in PCs long after it was useful, largely because operating systems still expected to be installed from one.

blocks.name: CD-ROM
blocks.text: A single disc held more than most hard drives of the time, which is what made large software possible: full motion video, recorded speech and orchestral music all arrived on the PC because there was finally somewhere to put them.

blocks.title: Capacity races ahead of speed
blocks.text: Through the nineties drive capacity grew faster than almost anything else in the machine, roughly doubling every eighteen months. Rotational speed went from 3600 rpm to 7200 and stopped, because spinning a metal platter faster costs power, generates heat and reduces reliability. The gap between how much a drive held and how fast it could deliver it kept widening.

blocks.name: Typical desktop drive
blocks.text: Fast enough that loading a program felt like a pause rather than a wait, which had not been true a few years earlier.

blocks.name: Seagate ST3491A
blocks.spec: 428 MB, IDE, 3600 rpm, ~14 ms seek, ~3 MB/s
blocks.text: Approaching half a gigabyte. Sequential transfer around 3 MB/s, which is where the storage speed test below starts.

blocks.name: EIDE and UDMA
blocks.text: Faster signalling on the same connector, and support for drives over 528 MB, a limit that had been quietly built into the earlier standard and caught everyone by surprise.

blocks.name: DVD-ROM
blocks.text: Seven times a CD. Games began shipping on one disc instead of five, and PCs started being used to watch films.

blocks.name: 7200 rpm becomes normal
blocks.text: The speed most desktop drives would run at for the next twenty years. Seek time settled around 9 milliseconds and stayed there.

blocks.name: ATA/100
blocks.text: The cable gained forty extra wires that carry no data, sitting between the signal wires to stop them interfering with each other. A reminder that at higher speeds the cable itself becomes the problem.

blocks.title: A thinner cable, and then no moving parts at all
blocks.text: SATA replaced the ribbon cable with a thin serial connection, which helped airflow and allowed higher speeds. Then flash memory arrived on the desktop, and for the first time storage had no mechanical delay to design around.

blocks.name: SATA 1.5 Gb/s
blocks.text: The wide ribbon cable had been in PCs since 1986 and blocked airflow across the whole case. SATA replaced forty wires with seven.

blocks.name: Western Digital Raptor
blocks.text: A server drive sold to enthusiasts, spinning at 10,000 rpm to cut the wait for the platter to come round. Expensive, small, loud, and the fastest storage available to a desktop for several years.

blocks.name: First consumer SSDs
blocks.text: Early drives were small, costly, and some were slower than a hard disk at sustained writing because the controllers were poor. The response time was already in a different league.

blocks.name: Intel X25-M
blocks.spec: 80 GB, SATA, 250 MB/s read, 0.085 ms access
blocks.text: The drive that made solid state storage credible. Its controller handled many requests at once instead of queueing them, and access time was roughly a hundred times better than any hard disk. Upgrading to one made an old computer feel new in a way no processor upgrade did.

blocks.name: SATA 6 Gb/s
blocks.text: Doubling the interface speed bought a few years. Flash memory was about to outgrow a connector designed around spinning disks.

blocks.title: Straight into the processor's own lanes
blocks.text: SATA was built for devices that took milliseconds to answer, so its command system assumed the drive was the slow part. NVMe threw that out and let a drive connect directly to the PCI Express lanes the processor uses for graphics, with thousands of parallel request queues instead of one.

blocks.name: NVMe and M.2
blocks.text: M.2 is the small slot on the board, NVMe is the language spoken over it. Together they removed the cable, the separate power connector and the drive bay, and the whole drive became a stick the size of a stick of gum.

blocks.name: Samsung 950 Pro
blocks.spec: 512 GB, PCIe 3.0 x4, 2,500 MB/s read, 0.05 ms
blocks.text: Five times the sequential speed of the fastest SATA drive, in a smaller package that needed no cable.

blocks.name: Samsung 970 EVO Plus
blocks.spec: 1 TB, PCIe 3.0 x4, 3,500 MB/s read, 0.05 ms
blocks.text: The point where NVMe drives became the default rather than the upgrade, because the price per gigabyte had fallen close to SATA.

blocks.name: WD Black SN850
blocks.text: Fast enough that games began to be designed assuming assets could be streamed from storage during play rather than loaded up front. The consoles released in 2020 made the same assumption.

blocks.name: Crucial T700
blocks.text: These drives need heatsinks. A component with no moving parts now produces enough heat to require the same cooling treatment as a processor did in 1995.

blocks.name: Where the bottleneck went
blocks.text: Sequential speed has improved about four thousand times since 1994. Access time has improved about three hundred and fifty times, and almost all of that came from one change, which was deleting the moving parts.

blocks.title: The same file, four decades apart
blocks.text: Pick a file size and two drives. The bars run at the drives' real measured speeds, with a seek penalty added for anything with an arm to move.

blocks.label: What filled the drives
blocks.text: Capacity grew about a million times. Install sizes grew at almost exactly the same rate.
